items.name: Mundigak, Shahr-i Sokhta and the Oxus traders
items.description: Mundigak, a mound north-west of Kandahar excavated by Jean-Marie Casal in 1951–1958, was a farming village by the 4th millennium BCE and by about 2500 BCE a walled town with a pillared 'palace' and a temple, painted pottery and seals that link it to Shahr-i Sokhta across the Iranian border in Sistan and to the Indus valley; together they form what archaeologists call the Helmand civilisation. The town declined in the 2nd millennium BCE. In the far north, on the Amu Darya, Shortugai was an outpost of the Harappan (Indus) civilisation from about 2200 BCE, probably there for the lapis lazuli of Badakhshan, the only source used in the ancient Near East and Egypt. The Bronze Age Oxus civilisation (BMAC) reached Bactria too; the Tillya Tepe and Dashly sites near Sheberghan belong to it.

items.name: Bactria, Aria and Arachosia under the Persians
items.description: Cyrus the Great (c. 550–530 BCE) brought the lands of today's Afghanistan into the Achaemenid Empire; Darius I's Behistun inscription (c. 520 BCE) lists Bactria (Balkh), Aria (Herat), Arachosia (Harauvatish, around Kandahar), Drangiana (Sistan) and Gandhara among his provinces. Old Kandahar, Bactra and Herat were satrapal capitals, and Bactrian and Arachosian levies fought at Gaugamela in 331 BCE. The Avesta, Zoroastrianism's scripture, names several of these lands, and later tradition placed Zoroaster himself at Balkh.

items.name: Alexander, the Mauryas and Greco-Bactria
items.description: Alexander the Great marched through Aria, Drangiana and Arachosia in 330–329 BCE, founding Alexandria in Arachosia (Kandahar) and Alexandria in the Caucasus (near Bagram), crossed the Hindu Kush and spent 329–327 BCE subduing Bactria and Sogdiana, where he married Roxana. The Seleucids ceded Arachosia and the Paropamisadae to Chandragupta Maurya in about 305 BCE, and the emperor Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE) set up edicts in Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar. In Bactria the satrap Diodotus broke away in about 250 BCE and founded the Greco-Bactrian kingdom, whose city of Ai-Khanoum on the Oxus had a theatre, a gymnasium and Delphic maxims carved in stone. Its kings crossed the Hindu Kush into India (the Indo-Greeks) before nomads, the Yuezhi among them, overran Bactria around 145–130 BCE.

items.name: The Kushans: Begram, Surkh Kotal and Gandharan art
items.description: The Yuezhi, nomads driven west from China, settled in Bactria after about 130 BCE; one of their five clans, the Kushans, united them under Kujula Kadphises in the 1st century CE and spread south over the Hindu Kush into Gandhara and northern India. Under Kanishka (c. 127–150) the empire ran from the Oxus to the Ganges, with capitals at Kapisa (Begram), Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura. The Rabatak inscription, found in Baghlan in 1993, records his reign in Bactrian written in Greek letters; the dynastic temple at Surkh Kotal and the Begram hoard of Indian ivories, Chinese lacquer and Roman glass show the trade that crossed Afghanistan. Gandharan Buddhist art, mixing Greek and Indian styles, flourished. The Tillya Tepe gold hoard (1st century BCE–1st century CE) comes from nomad graves near Sheberghan. The Sasanians took Bactria in the 3rd century, ruling it through Kushanshahs.

items.name: Huns, Nezaks and the Buddhas of Bamiyan
items.description: From about 370 'Iranian Huns' replaced the Kushanshahs: first the Kidarites, then the Alchon Huns, who struck coins at Kabul and invaded India, the Hephthalites in Bactria (from about 466) and the Nezak kings of Kabul and Zabul. Buddhism still thrived. In the Bamiyan valley two colossal Buddhas, 38 and 55 metres high, were cut into the cliff; radiocarbon dating places them around 570 and 618, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang described them gilded and glittering when he passed in 630. Monasteries such as Fondukistan near Ghorband and Tepe Shotor at Hadda near Jalalabad have yielded clay sculpture of this age. After the Hephthalites fell to the Turks and Persians (557–560), the Western Turks' yabghus ruled Tokharistan, and the Nezaks held Kabul until a Turkic dynasty, the Turk Shahis, replaced them around 665.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Cultural Landscape and Archaeological Remains of the Bamiyan Valley

items.name: Turk and Hindu Shahis, the Zunbils and the Arabs
items.description: The Arabs took Herat, Balkh and Zaranj in the 650s, but beyond them they met two dynasties that held them off for two centuries. The Turk Shahis, a Turkic dynasty that took over Kabul and Gandhara from the Nezaks around 665, ruled from Kabul and Udabhandapura (Hund) on the Indus. A branch, the Zunbils, broke away around 680 and ruled Zabulistan (around Ghazni), Arachosia and Zamindawar; they destroyed an Arab 'Army of Destruction' in 698 and in 700 provoked Ibn al-Ash'ath's revolt. The Tang emperors invested both kings. Around 822 the Turk Shahi king was overthrown by his Brahmin minister Kallar, founding the Hindu Shahis. The Saffarid Ya'qub ibn al-Layth killed the Zunbil in 865 and took Zabul and Kabul around 870, so the Hindu Shahis withdrew to Gandhara; their king Jayapala lost to Mahmud of Ghazni at Peshawar in 1001, and his successors were driven from the Salt Range and Lahore by 1021, the line ending about 1026.

items.name: The Saffarids of Sistan
items.description: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar, a coppersmith who led volunteer fighters in Sistan, seized Zaranj in 861. He took Herat from the Tahirids in 867, killed the Zunbil and took Kabul and Bamiyan by 870, and took Nishapur and Fars before the caliph's army stopped him at Dayr al-Aqul near Baghdad in 876. Persian, not Arabic, was used at his court. His brother Amr ruled Khurasan until the Samanid Isma'il defeated and captured him near Balkh in 900; after that the Saffarids held only Sistan, under the Samanids and then independently, until Mahmud of Ghazni deposed the last of them, Khalaf ibn Ahmad, in 1003.

items.name: The Ghaznavids: Mahmud of Ghazni and Ferdowsi
items.description: Sabuktigin, a Turkic slave soldier, became governor of Ghazni for the Samanids in 977 and took Bost the same year. His son Mahmud (998–1030) took Khurasan from the Samanids in 999 and turned Ghazni into one of the richest courts in the Islamic world: Ferdowsi finished the Shahnameh for him in 1010, and the scholar al-Biruni travelled with his armies and wrote his study of India. Mahmud raided northern India some seventeen times, sacking Somnath in 1025, and annexed the Punjab with Lahore in about 1021. His son Mas'ud lost Khurasan to the Seljuks at Dandanaqan in 1040. The later Ghaznavids ruled from Ghazni and Lahore, building the winter palaces of Lashkari Bazar near Bost, until the Ghurid Ala al-Din Husayn burned Ghazni in 1150–1151 and Oghuz Turks took it in 1163; the last sultan, Khusrau Malik, lost Lahore to Muhammad of Ghor in 1186.

items.name: The Ghurids and the Minaret of Jam
items.description: Ghor, the mountain heart of Afghanistan, was conquered by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1011, and its Shansabanid chiefs ruled under the Ghaznavids and Seljuks. Ala al-Din Husayn, 'the World Burner', sacked Ghazni in 1150–1151, and his nephews Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad (1163–1203) and Mu'izz al-Din Muhammad of Ghor made Ghor an empire: Ghazni in 1173, Herat in 1175, Peshawar in 1179, Lahore in 1186 and, after victory at Tarain in 1192, Delhi in 1193. A branch ruled Bamiyan and Tokharistan. The summer capital Firozkoh is lost, but its 65-metre Minaret of Jam (c. 1190s), covered in brick patterns and Quranic verses, still stands in a remote gorge; Ghiyath also rebuilt Herat's Friday Mosque. After the Khwarazmshah beat Mu'izz at Andkhud (1204) and Mu'izz was assassinated (1206), his Turkish generals kept India (the Delhi Sultanate) and the Khwarazmshahs took Herat, Ghor and finally Ghazni (1215).

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Minaret and Archaeological Remains of Jam

items.name: Genghis Khan, the Kartids and the ruin of the cities
items.description: Genghis Khan's war on the Khwarazmshahs reached Afghanistan in 1220–1222. Balkh surrendered and was destroyed; at Bamiyan, where his grandson Mutukan was killed, the valley was put to the sword and the town on the citadel of Shahr-i Gholghola was razed; Herat rebelled and was sacked in 1222. Jalal al-Din Mangburni beat a Mongol army at Parwan in 1221 before Genghis chased him to the Indus. Herat recovered under the Kartids, Tajik maliks from Ghor whom the Mongols made rulers of Herat in 1245; under the Ilkhans they ruled Herat, Ghor and much of the east, and after the Ilkhanate collapsed (1335) they ruled independently. The Qara'unas Mongols held the east and north. Timur took Herat in 1381 and ended the dynasty in 1389.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire

items.name: Timurid Herat: Gawhar Shad, Jami and Bihzad
items.description: Timur conquered Afghanistan in 1381–1383. His son Shah Rukh (1405–1447) made Herat the capital of the Timurid empire, and with his wife Gawhar Shad turned it into a centre of Persian art: her musalla complex with its minarets and mausoleum (1417–1438) still partly stands. The city's golden age came under Sultan Husayn Bayqara (1469–1506), whose minister Ali-Shir Nava'i wrote Chagatai Turkic poetry, while the poet Jami and the miniature painter Kamal ud-Din Bihzad worked at his court. Husayn rebuilt the shrine at Mazar-i Sharif in 1481. Herat fell to the Uzbek Muhammad Shaybani in 1507.

items.name: Babur's Kabul, the Mughals, the Safavids and the Uzbeks
items.description: Babur, a Timurid prince driven from Fergana, took Kabul in 1504 and ruled from it for 22 years; he took Kandahar from the Arghuns in 1522, and from Kabul he invaded India, founding the Mughal Empire at Panipat in 1526. He asked to be buried in his garden at Kabul, the Bagh-e Babur. For two centuries Afghanistan was divided: Kabul and the east were a Mughal province (ruled by Babur's grandson Mirza Hakim until 1585), Herat and the west belonged to Safavid Persia, and Balkh and the north to the Uzbek khans of Bukhara (who also held Herat in 1588–1598). Kandahar, the key to both empires, changed hands repeatedly: Safavid in 1558, Mughal in 1595, Safavid in 1622, Mughal in 1638 and Safavid from 1649, after three failed Mughal sieges. Shah Jahan's armies occupied Balkh in 1646–1647 but could not hold it.

items.name: The Hotaks: Mirwais and the fall of Isfahan
items.description: In 1709 Mirwais Hotak, chief of the Ghilji Pashtuns, killed the Safavid governor of Kandahar, the Georgian Gurgin Khan, and made Kandahar independent. His son Mahmud invaded Persia, beat the Safavid army at Gulnabad in March 1722 and after a six-month siege took Isfahan in October; Shah Sultan Husayn abdicated to him. Mahmud and his cousin Ashraf ruled Isfahan, Kerman and Fars, but Ottoman and Russian armies took Persia's western and northern provinces, and in 1729 Nader Quli Khan, general of the Safavid prince Tahmasp, drove the Afghans out of Persia. Herat meanwhile had its own Abdali (Durrani) rulers from 1717 until Nader took it in 1732. Mirwais's son Hussain held Kandahar until Nader Shah took it in March 1738 after a year-long siege, and Nader went on to sack Delhi.

items.name: Ahmad Shah Durrani's empire
items.description: When Nader Shah was assassinated in June 1747, the commander of his Abdali cavalry, Ahmad Khan, was chosen king at a jirga near Kandahar and took the title Durr-i Durran, 'pearl of pearls'; his Abdali tribe became the Durranis. He took Kabul and Peshawar in 1747–1748, Herat in 1750 and the lands north of the Hindu Kush in 1751, and won the Punjab, Kashmir and Sindh as tributaries from the weakened Mughals. His victory over the Marathas at Panipat in 1761 was one of the largest battles of the century, but the Sikhs took Lahore in 1765. His empire, the forerunner of modern Afghanistan, reached from Mashhad to Kashmir and from the Amu Darya to the Arabian Sea. His son Timur Shah moved the capital from Kandahar to Kabul in 1776; Timur's sons fought one another for the throne (Zaman, Mahmud, Shuja), losing Kashmir to the Sikhs in 1819 and breaking up by 1823.

items.name: Dost Mohammad, the Anglo-Afghan wars and independence
items.description: Dost Mohammad Khan of the Barakzai family made himself emir at Kabul in 1826. Fearing Russian influence, the British invaded in 1839 to restore Shah Shuja; Kabul rose in 1841, and the British army's retreat from Kabul in January 1842 ended in its destruction in the passes, though a punitive force returned briefly. Dost Mohammad, restored, took Balkh, Kandahar and finally Herat (1863). In the Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878–1880) the British won at Kandahar despite their defeat at Maiwand, and left Abdur Rahman Khan as emir under British control of foreign policy. 'The Iron Emir' (1880–1901) crushed revolts, conquered the Hazarajat (1891–1893) and Kafiristan (1895–1896, renamed Nuristan) and accepted the Durand Line with British India (1893); the Wakhan corridor was added in 1895 to separate Russia and India. After the Third Anglo-Afghan War, the Treaty of Rawalpindi (1919) recognised Afghanistan's full independence.

items.name: Amanullah, Zahir Shah and the kingdom
items.description: King Amanullah Khan (1919–1929) tried to modernise the country on Turkish lines, with a first constitution (1923), schools for girls and the unveiling of women, until a revolt in 1928–1929 put the Tajik bandit Habibullah Kalakani on the throne for nine months. Mohammed Nadir Shah took Kabul back in October 1929 and was assassinated in 1933; his son Mohammed Zahir Shah reigned for forty years, keeping Afghanistan neutral in the Second World War and taking aid from both the USSR and the United States (the Helmand valley dams, the Salang tunnel of 1964). The 1964 constitution brought an elected parliament and a free press. In 1973 his cousin Mohammed Daoud Khan abolished the monarchy and declared a republic.

items.name: Coup, Soviet war, civil war and the Taliban
items.description: In the Saur Revolution of April 1978 the communist People's Democratic Party killed Daoud and seized power; its land reforms and purges set off revolts, and in December 1979 the Soviet Union invaded, killing Hafizullah Amin and installing Babrak Karmal. Some 5–6 million Afghans fled to Pakistan and Iran, and mujahideen armed by the US, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia fought the Soviet army until it withdrew in February 1989. Mohammad Najibullah's government fell in April 1992, and the mujahideen factions then fought over Kabul, destroying much of it. The Taliban, a movement of religious students, took Kandahar in 1994 and Kabul in September 1996, imposing a harsh Islamic emirate; in March 2001 they blew up the Buddhas of Bamiyan. Al-Qaeda, sheltered by them, carried out the attacks of 11 September 2001, and US-led forces and the Northern Alliance drove the Taliban from power in October–December 2001.

items.name: The Islamic Republic and the Taliban's return
items.description: After the Bonn Agreement of December 2001 Hamid Karzai led an interim government; a new constitution (2004) created the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, and Karzai won the first presidential election that year. Millions of refugees returned and girls went back to school, but the Taliban insurgency revived from 2005, and NATO's ISAF mission, with up to about 130,000 troops, handed security to Afghan forces in 2014. Ashraf Ghani succeeded Karzai in 2014. The US–Taliban Doha agreement of February 2020 set a foreign withdrawal; as the last troops left, the Taliban swept the provinces and entered Kabul on 15 August 2021, while Ghani fled. The restored Islamic Emirate has barred girls from secondary school and university and women from most work.
